newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil telecom stocks seen higher on cellular bids.
newsitem.headline: Brazil telecom stocks seen higher on cellular bids.

text.p: Brazilian telecommunications stocks will get a boost if investors pay much above the base price set for the auctions of Band B cellular concessions, said a telecom analyst at Banco Pactual.
"Telebras' units may reach higher market price levels depending on the price investors pay for the Band B concessions," said analyst Eduardo Munemori.

The Brazilian government, which will be receiving bids from investors early next month, set a 3.7 billion real base price for concessions to operate cellular services on the Band B frequency in 10 regions nationwide.

The minimum price for concessions for metropolitan Sao Paulo and Sao Paulo state was set at 600 million reais each, while the contract for Rio de Janeiro and Espirito Santo states had a base price of 500 million reais. Each of the other seven concessions have lower base prices.
"If investors decide to pay much more than the base price to build a new service, imagine how much they can pay for what is already established," he told reporters, referring to the Telebras system.
Munemori noted telecommunications stocks surged after the sale of a strategic stake in Rio Grande do Sul state's Companhia Riograndense de Telecomunicacoes (CRT) in December last year.
The stake in CRT was bought by a group including Telefonica de Espana and Brazil's RBS for a price that was 54.8 percent above the base set by Rio Grande do Sul state.

So far at least 13 consortia, including local and foreign investors, have been formally assembled to bid on the Band B concessions, Munemori told reporters before speaking at a seminar on telecoms privatizations.
Munemori also said he does not expect a delay in the bidding process despite uncertainties over a court ruling that could hurt the government's plans to privatize the Band B cellular services.

The Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF), Brazil's highest court, is due to rule on the constitutionality of the so-called Minimum Telecommunications Law, which the government introduced in 1996 as a legal framework for its plan to tender the Band B concessions.
The supreme court, which has delayed ruling on the case several times, has not yet set a new date to resume deliberations.

Munemori said an eventual delay in the Band B bidding process could raise the value of the Telebras system, as the company would gain time to invest in the cellular market and increase its competitiveness.
